title: Addressing stationarity violations in double‐observer drone surveys: A koala case study
content:
Independent drone observers survey the same area with a temporal offset. Movement between passes violates stationarity, causing re-detections of the same individual to be misclassified as independent observations and inflating abundance estimates. Incorporating movement information using a hidden Markov model links plausible re-detections and reduces this bias, with direct consequences for conservation-relevant abundance estimates.


Abstract

Robust estimation of animal abundance depends on survey designs that minimise assumption violations and analytical approaches that correct those that remain. In double-observer protocols, stationarity is violated when individuals move between repeat passes, generating two independent detections instead of a single joint detection and inflating multinomial capture histories. Hidden Markov models (HMMs) fitted to independent telemetry data provide a principled way to quantify this violation, replacing binary spatial matching thresholds with probabilistic, movement-informed detection assignments. We evaluated how stationarity assumptions embedded in double-observer multinomial abundance models affect estimates of koala (Phascolarctos cinereus) abundance, detection probability and covariate inference when applied to identical drone survey data. Drone surveys were conducted at 169 sites, with two independent observers per flight. Data were analysed using two Bayesian hierarchical multinomial double-observer models: one applying a strict spatial detection-matching criterion (Multinomial-P) and one incorporating HMM-derived probabilities fitted to koala telemetry data (Multinomial-P HMM) independently obtained from nearby locations. Both models included key covariates on detection and abundance. Mean per-visit detection probability was slightly higher under the HMM model (0.586, 95% CrI: 0.492–0.693) than under the strict matching model (0.520, 95% CrI: 0.426–0.625), although credible intervals overlapped substantially. Canopy height positively influenced detection and wind speed negatively influenced detection in both models. Air temperature had a positive effect, while survey date showed no credible effect. The strict spatial criterion produced higher abundance estimates (893 koalas, 95% CrI: 760–1053) than the HMM-informed approach (734 koalas, 95% CrI: 634–853). Bayesian contrast showed a median difference of +160 koalas (95% CrI: −15 to +348; P[Strict > HMM] = 0.96), consistent with an increase from movement-induced misclassification, although the interval marginally included zero. Soil depth negatively predicted local abundance and vegetation productivity positively predicted abundance, with effect sizes consistent across models. Detection-matching criteria influenced total abundance estimates, with the strict spatial approach producing estimates about 22% higher than the HMM approach, while detection and covariate inference remained robust. Practical implication: Model assumption violations matter for conservation decisions where abundance thresholds trigger management action responses.
